new_sources.title: Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, "Land as pedagogy: Nishnaabeg intelligence and rebellious transformation," Decolonization: Indigeneity, Education & Society 3, no. 3 (2014): 1–25.
new_sources.citation: Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, "Land as pedagogy: Nishnaabeg intelligence and rebellious transformation," Decolonization: Indigeneity, Education & Society 3, no. 3 (2014): 1–25.

verification.note: Open access (CC BY-NC 3.0); pages 1, 3–4, 12–14, 17, 19–20 and 22–23 read. Resurgence 'the rebuilding of Indigenous nations according to our own political, intellectual and cultural traditions' and the turn from efforts to 'Indigenize the academy' toward 'a resurgence of Indigenous intellectual systems' (p. 22); 'This colonial refusal should be met with Indigenous refusal' (p. 22), with n. 41 citing Coulthard on recognition and Audra Simpson on refusal; drafts reviewed outside standard academic peer review (n. 1). Passages reporting Elders' teachings and oral history are not used (OCAP limits).

new_sources.title: Haunani-Kay Trask, "Natives and Anthropologists: The Colonial Struggle," The Contemporary Pacific 3, no. 1 (1991): 159–167.
new_sources.citation: Haunani-Kay Trask, "Natives and Anthropologists: The Colonial Struggle," The Contemporary Pacific 3, no. 1 (Spring 1991): 159–167.

verification.note: Read in full in the University of Hawaiʻi institutional repository (also JSTOR 23701492). self-description as a Hawaiian (p. 159); genealogy as 'Native forms of history' (p. 160); 'Natives don't know very much … thus there is no need to read them' as a shared academic assumption (p. 160); 'from historians and anthropologists to bureaucrats and politicians' (p. 164); 'We do not need, nor do we want to be "liberated" from our past' (p. 164); a passage of Hawaiian knowledge quoted there from Kameʻeleihiwa is not used (OCAP limits); the Kahoʻolawe report (p. 166 n. 4).

new_sources.citation: Roger M. Keesing, "Reply to Trask," The Contemporary Pacific 3, no. 1 (Spring 1991): 168–171.

verification.note: Pages 168–170 read. The 'insider' versus 'outsider' dichotomy 'a great leap backward' (p. 168); battle lines of 'class and interest' (p. 168); 'Is it really necessary … to edit out human sacrifice, chiefly oppression, bloody wars, patriarchy?' (p. 169).

new_sources.title: D'Arcy McNickle, Native American Tribalism (OUP, 1973; 1993 reissue with Peter Iverson's introduction), publisher preview.
new_sources.citation: D'Arcy McNickle, Native American Tribalism: Indian Survivals and Renewals (New York: Oxford University Press, 1973; reissued 1993 with an introduction by Peter Iverson).

verification.note: OUP publisher preview: Iverson's introduction pp. iii–v, xvii–xviii and McNickle's preface pp. xix–xx read. Born 18 January 1904 (p. iii; Wikidata gives 14 January, so the year only is used); role in founding the NCAI, 1944, and 'few Native historians have tried to provide an overview of the national Indian experience' (p. iv); chaired the 1961 Chicago conference steering committee, died 1977, Newberry centre's first fellows 1973–74 with McNickle as director, Hoxie's 1992 remark as reported (p. v); Preface: 'the certainty that native America had vanished before the march of progress'; 'Indians had no future as Indians' (pp. xix–xx). Iverson's p. iv attribution of They Came Here First to Collier is an error and is not adopted.

new_sources.title: Audra Simpson, "On Ethnographic Refusal: Indigeneity, 'Voice' and Colonial Citizenship," Junctures 9 (2007): 67–80.
new_sources.citation: Audra Simpson, "On Ethnographic Refusal: Indigeneity, 'Voice' and Colonial Citizenship," Junctures: The Journal for Thematic Dialogue 9 (December 2007): 67–80.

verification.note: Read in full in the journal's own open-access PDF, pp. 67–80 and notes 1–28 (footer 'Junctures, 9, Dec 2007'). Passages used: 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm that evacuates theory' (pp. 70–71); Iroquois studies 'a documentary form' seeking 'to authenticate cultural forms rather than analyse them' (p. 71); refusal as 'a calculus … of what you need to know and what I refuse to write in' (p. 72); 'never properly "post-colonial"' (p. 68); no doubleness 'that Fanon, Bhabha and Giddens speak of' (p. 74); 'the punctuating, juridical bestowals of settler colonialism' (p. 74); history-writing 'naturalises this occupation' (p. 75); credits Moreton-Robinson (p. 69) and Alfred's books (p. 78 n. 28). Interview passages are not used (OCAP limits). Wolfe appears only as a supporting citation (n. 3). Author note: assistant professor, Cornell (p. 80).

new_sources.title: Fiona Nicoll, "Interrupting White Possession and Unsettling State Borders: Expanding Frontiers of Critical Indigenous Studies," International Journal of Critical Indigenous Studies 8, no. 1 (2015): 47–59.
new_sources.citation: Fiona Nicoll, "Interrupting White Possession and Unsettling State Borders: Expanding Frontiers of Critical Indigenous Studies," review essay on Aileen Moreton-Robinson, The White Possessive (2015), and Audra Simpson, Mohawk Interruptus (2014), International Journal of Critical Indigenous Studies 8, no. 1 (2015): 47–59.

verification.note: Open-access PDF on the journal platform, read in full (13 pp.). A named reader (cultural studies, University of Queensland). Quotations of both books are Nicoll's, with her page references (e.g. Mohawk Interruptus pp. 3, 13, 85, 93, 94; The White Possessive p. xiii); neither book read at first hand. Journal DOI not checked.

new_sources.title: Glen Sean Coulthard, "Subjects of Empire? Indigenous Peoples and the 'Politics of Recognition' in Canada" (PhD diss., University of Victoria, 2009).
new_sources.citation: Glen Sean Coulthard, "Subjects of Empire? Indigenous Peoples and the 'Politics of Recognition' in Canada" (PhD dissertation, Department of Political Science, University of Victoria, 2009).

verification.note: UVic institutional repository PDF (issued 30 November 2009), read in part: abstract pp. iv–v; acknowledgements (Tully and Alfred as mentors); introduction pp. 1–2, 11–20, 27–28; chapter openings pp. 74–75 and 158–160. Passages used: 'to challenge the now commonplace assumption that the colonial relationship … can be reconciled via such a politics of recognition' (abstract); Taylor quoted as the influential statement (p. 28); 'Canada is no different than any other settler-colonial power' (p. 11); primitive accumulation's 'excessively temporal framing' (p. 13); 'dispossession, not proletarianization' (p. 20); Fanon 'fails to push us far enough' (p. 160). The 2014 book revises this text; quotations here are dated 2009. Wolfe is not cited in the pages read.

new_sources.title: Chris Andersen, "Métis": Race, Recognition, and the Struggle for Indigenous Peoplehood (UBC Press, 2014), publisher sample.
new_sources.citation: Chris Andersen, "Métis": Race, Recognition, and the Struggle for Indigenous Peoplehood (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2014); publisher sample of the front matter and introduction.

verification.note: Publisher sample (https://www.ubcpress.ca/asset/9519/1/9780774827218.pdf) read: introduction pp. 3–20. Passages used: 'simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity that seem to fascinate so many scholars who write of Métis histories' (p. 5); the historian Brenda Macdougall quoted (pp. 5–6); 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?' and 'our communities and our peoplehood' (p. 10); racialization part of 'a larger set of colonial projects' to 'usurp all the Indigenous territories' (pp. 10–11); 'a "national core" historically located in Red River' (p. 13); 'History is thus a crucial resource in Indigenous claims to peoplehood' (p. 20). Chapters 1–5, where named fur-trade historians are discussed, unread. Ebook 12 May 2014; paperback 15 January 2015.

new_sources.title: Chris Andersen, "Critical Indigenous Studies: From Difference to Density," Cultural Studies Review 15, no. 2 (2009): 80–100.
new_sources.citation: Chris Andersen, "Critical Indigenous Studies: From Difference to Density," Cultural Studies Review 15, no. 2 (September 2009): 80–100.

verification.note: Open access (UTS ePress); pp. 80–82, 90–92, 95–97 read. A 'sympathetic critique' of Duane Champagne (p. 81); Indigenous communities as 'knowers not just of Indigeneity, but of whiteness as well' (pp. 90–91); communities use history, e.g. 'archival documents to assist them in legal battles' (p. 95). Author note: 'CHRIS ANDERSEN is Michif (Métis) from western Canada' (p. 97).

row.context: Writer and scholar: resurgence as 'the rebuilding of Indigenous nations according to our own political, intellectual and cultural traditions'; a turn from efforts to 'Indigenize the academy'; 'This colonial refusal should be met with Indigenous refusal' (2014, read), citing Coulthard on recognition and Audra Simpson on refusal.
row.works: Dancing on Our Turtle's Back (2011); 'Land as pedagogy' (2014); As We Have Always Done (2017)

row.context: Audra Simpson (2007, read) drew on her account of 'differential access to power and historical knowing' and terra nullius; The White Possessive (2015) is known through Nicoll's review, which quotes the introduction: white possession is 'hypervisible' to Indigenous people.
row.works: Talkin' Up to the White Woman (2000); The White Possessive (2015)

row.context: A shared reference of the resurgence writers, not read here: Coulthard names him a mentor (2009); Audra Simpson places his books among the work of 'a cadre of scholars from Kahnawake' (2007, n. 28); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson cites him (2014).
row.works: Heeding the Voices of Our Ancestors (1995); Peace, Power, Righteousness (1999); Wasáse (2005)
